page_title: Operating a Large, Distributed System in a Reliable Way: Practices I Learned

sources.entry: Operating a Large, Distributed System in a Reliable Way: Practices I Learned, Gergely Orosz.

summary.title: Operating a Large, Distributed System in a Reliable Way: Practices I Learned
summary.one_liner: A practical tour of how Uber's payments team operates a large distributed system reliably, covering monitoring, on-call, incident handling, postmortems, failover drills, SLOs and SRE team structure.
takeaways: Monitor traffic, errors, latency (use p95/p99/p999, not averages) and saturation, plus business-level metrics that show whether key user flows actually work.
Make service teams own their on-call, use runbooks attached to alerts, and track alert signal-to-noise to avoid burnout.
During an outage, mitigate first (e.g., roll back) and defer root-cause investigation until later; use blameless postmortems with 5 Whys to find systemic fixes.
Run regular data center failover drills and black-box tests, since failover can overload the target DC and cause cascading failures.
Define service-level SLOs (capacity, latency, accuracy, availability) and roll them up into SLAs; a dedicated SRE team usually becomes necessary as reliability work grows.
summary.summary: The author, who has worked on Uber's payments system for several years, shares practices learned from operating a large distributed system with frequent deploys and global traffic. The post walks through monitoring (infrastructure, service health, latency percentiles, business metrics), on-call and alerting, outage handling, postmortems and incident reviews, failover drills, planned downtime, black-box testing, and capacity planning. It then covers SLOs versus SLAs, the role of an SRE team, and reliability as ongoing investment, with concrete examples such as a 5 Whys walkthrough and an example SLO table. The author notes the practices may be overkill for smaller or less critical systems.
